paragraphs: Three days after the spring banquet, Yao Chang held a wedding in the rear courtyard of his house.

The courtyard was small, with room for only a few tables. Lamb had been simmering in the kitchen since dawn; pale smoke curled past the grape arbor and climbed the eaves. An old servant had cut the red characters for double happiness, but the scissors were blunt, and one character came out fat, the other thin. Pasted on the door, they lent the house a cheerfulness of their own. Yao Chang put on a freshly washed leather robe and stood at the entrance, welcoming every guest himself. At the weddings of Chang’an’s wealthy families, gold and silver vessels were indispensable. Here there were only wooden platters and earthenware cups, and the wine was rough enough to warm a man’s brow after two bowls.

Lei Edi arrived leading his son’s horse, with five or six old acquaintances from the Qiang lands behind him. Father and son seldom came to the capital. When the old man saw that Yao’s house had none of the ceremony displayed at the gates of an official residence, he felt somewhat easier.

The groom, Lei Ding, was a sturdy young man who bowed deeply to his bride’s elder relatives. The bride, a woman of the Yao family, emerged from behind the curtain with red silk over her face and tiny white flowers embroidered along her cuffs. Her mother had died early, and she had grown up in the household of Yao Chang’s elder brother. Before leaving, she had insisted on packing an old felt coat in her bridal chest. The elderly woman conducting the wedding had complained that its color was faded. The bride merely said that when winter came in Anding, no quantity of gold or silk could replace its warmth.
When Yao Chang heard, he laughed. “Let her take the coat. The western wind doesn’t inspect a dowry.”

After a few cups, Lei Edi traced the rim of his bowl with one finger and sighed. “My eldest was sent to Liangzhou, serving under a Xianbei commandant. Last time he came home he told me they even have rules about who eats from which pot first. My third boy’s been repairing city walls. He writes asking me for measuring rods and cord, and every other word is about the Central Army’s regulations. When they were little, I taught them to ride. They could have found our pasture with their eyes shut. Now they hardly know how to speak Qiang.”
Yao Chang tore off a piece of lamb and passed it to him. “If they know the roads and speak the language used in camp, they’ll find fewer troubles away from home.”

“Fewer troubles?” Lei Edi gave him a sidelong look. “They look splendid in Qin armor, but when they see me they dare call me Father only in private. Your old soldiers have been broken up and sent elsewhere. Doesn’t that hurt you?”

Yao Chang did not push his cup forward for more wine. He watched the young couple exchanging their bows in the courtyard. A long while passed before he spoke. “I, too, had men who followed me for more than ten years. On the day they were sent away, every one of them wanted to keep his old horse. I told them to lead the horses to their new camps.”
“And you could bear it?”
“What would it have changed if I couldn’t? The court provides the grain and appoints the officers. Would it have been kindness to ask those men to die with me?”
Lei Edi drained his cup. The deep lines in his face relaxed, then drew tight once more. “Why, then, have you joined your house to mine in marriage today?”

Yao Chang looked toward the bride. She bowed to the elders of the Lei family, then lightly adjusted the hairpin in her hair as she rose, as if afraid of breaking something. Lei Ding held out a hand to steady her sleeve.
“A girl is getting married. The match belongs to her,” Yao Chang said. “You and I have known each other too long not to drink a cup of wine in her honor.”

Lei Edi was not a man easily soothed, yet after that he could hardly continue questioning him. That night he left no warhorse behind. He left only a young attendant named Lei Tong, ostensibly to care for the bride’s horses for several months so that she would be spared the worst jolts on the road to Anding. Yao Chang agreed, entered the young man as a groom in his household and paid him the customary wages.

Within three days, Lei Tong had learned the different grades of horse feed issued from the palace and which merchant caravans purchased leather for the Right Guard. Yao Chang never discussed affairs in the stables. From time to time he merely asked whether the Lei family was faring well. Lei Tong’s answers were always brief. The young man still thought of Yao Chang as an elder who could speak on behalf of his family.

In late spring the Shi family’s leather shop in the West Market delivered its accounts for the previous season. The proprietor was a Han man from Anding, surnamed Shi. He had polished the beads of his abacus bright with use, yet in Yao Chang’s presence he scarcely dared lift his head.

The ledger listed hides, saddles and packets of salt, each sum clearly entered. Near the end Yao Chang noticed that the fees for escorting goods through the passes had risen abruptly on two journeys. “Has the road to Anding fallen into disrepair?” he asked.

“The road is still there. They’ve added officials at the passes to inspect household registrations,” Shopkeeper Shi replied evasively. “Some porters don’t care to leave their names in the government records. That makes the journey difficult.”

Yao Chang closed the ledger and waited for him to go on. After a long hesitation, Shi admitted that officials had discovered four hundred and seventy-six unregistered people living on his elder brother’s estate. Three years of taxes were to be collected in arrears, and the younger inhabitants might also be conscripted. They had fled there in years of disaster, bringing old people and children. They had lived on the estate a long time, but in the official registers they still had no homes at all.
“Your brother has them work his fields. He owes taxes to the court,” Yao Chang said.

“I understand the principle, my lord,” Shi said urgently. “But how are the tenants supposed to pay three years’ taxes at once? My brother fears the authorities will arrest them, and he also fears they’ll flee in the night. If they scatter, those fields will lie waste next year.”
“Do they themselves want to stay?”
Shi blinked, plainly astonished by the question. “There’s food on the estate. Surely that’s better than the road.”
“Then let the registers be examined. Those who owe taxes must settle them, and those who need household registration must be entered.”
Shi’s face fell, and he reached for his accounts. But Yao Chang asked, “I hear some of the pasturelands in Longxi are short of laborers, and pay better than farming?”
“They are short, yes. But to go beyond the passes, a man needs documents.”

“A caravan may change its porters several times on one journey. That’s nothing unusual. If anyone wishes of his own accord to find other work, do not let your brother hold him prisoner on the estate.” Yao Chang pushed the account book back. “Merchants who use the public roads should keep proper records of their cargo and their men. We cannot have military supplies used to hide disgrace.”

Shi agreed over and over. By the time he left Yao’s residence, sweat had soaked through his clothes. He had understood the first part of the advice, and the second as well. Taken together, whether they amounted to a warning or a suggestion was more than he dared decide.

After that, the Shi family’s carts occasionally carried passengers westward with their leather goods. Some travelers had complete travel permits; others possessed papers bearing only assumed names. The checkpoint clerks were occupied inspecting samples of goods bound for the Right Guard, and sometimes, in rain or at dusk, failed to count everyone riding on the carts. Yao Chang’s household kept dates of dispatch, numbers of wagons and escort fees, but never made a separate secret register of names. A month later, if the Court of Justice wished to discover who had ridden in any particular wagon, its officials would have to piece together the records of relay stations, merchant shops and border checkpoints, one entry at a time.

At the beginning of the fourth month, fresh locust leaves at a Buddhist temple south of the city had grown broad enough to shade half a wall. Feng Chen lived in an eastern room behind the temple, copying scriptures each day and marking the hours by the bells. He had served the former state of Yan. When Qin took Hebei he lost his office, and the books sent by old friends filled half his room. Some scrolls still bore the handwriting of Yan officials. He could not bring himself to burn them.
When Yao Chang entered, Feng Chen was spreading a damp scroll in the corridor to dry.
“Has the Right Guard General come to seek the Buddha’s protection?” Feng Chen asked without rising.
“There’s been so much rain in Chang’an. I came to see whether your books might get wet again.”
“If that is why you came, General, you have more leisure than the censors.”

Yao Chang sat by the corridor. A young novice brought him weak tea. It was bitter, and he set it down after a single sip. Without circling the matter, he asked whether Feng Chen knew that some men in northern Dai had urged Murong Chui to restore Yan.
“I know.” Feng Chen lifted his fingers from the edge of the paper. “I heard he burned their flag.”
“Do you believe he could bear to let it go?”

“The flag was cloth. It took one night to burn. The places where his father and brothers lie buried—he could burn fires for ten years and still remember them.” Feng Chen turned the scroll over. “Yet he commands Qin soldiers now and fights Qin’s wars. Some men of the old Yan hate him for that. Others hope he will live. All their hopes together might not survive a single defeat.”
“And what of you, Master Feng?”
“I am old. I must give my destination in writing even to leave the city. All I ask is that no one burn these books in a single fire.”
Hearing this, Yao Chang lowered his eyes to the broken tea leaves floating on the surface of his cup. Suddenly Feng Chen asked, “Whom have you really come looking for today?”
“No one.”
“Then have you come to ask whether the men of the old Yan still remember where their hearts belong?”
“I fear only that when a man leaves his native land, a day may come when there is no one left even to bear witness for him.”

Feng Chen did not answer. He gazed at the slanting sunlight in the courtyard and remembered passing the palaces of Ye as a young man. Roses had covered the tops of those walls. Who could still name the flowers as they had been called in those days?
“General Yao,” he said, “there is nothing wrong with keeping another man’s past alive. Using that past to coax him into dying is the easiest thing in the world, and among the vilest.”
Yao Chang slowly set down his tea. “I shall remember those words, Master.”

That was the end of their conversation. Willow catkins were blowing outside the temple gate. When Yao Chang stepped into his carriage, several white tufts clung to his sleeves. Feng Chen stood on the steps watching him go. He did not feel he had taken part in any conspiracy. Yet what the two men had said that day was enough to be remembered in very different ways by different listeners.
The first thing Crown Prince Fu Hong noticed was a small discrepancy in the Right Guard’s monthly register.

Commandant Lü An had taken leave in the second month to mourn his mother. In the fourth month he had reported his birth mother gravely ill. Both village certificates bore official marks. Fu Hong examined them for a long while, then summoned the clerk in charge. “I did not know a man’s own mother could fall ill after she had died.”

The clerk dropped to his knees in fright and protested that there must have been a copying error. Fu Hong did not immediately order Lü An arrested. He asked first for the horses, relay lodgings and attendants used on both journeys to be checked. The fodder slips kept at the relay stations did not show Lü An’s name at all for the journey in the second month. Instead, a packhorse belonging to a Longxi caravan had used a Right Guard credential to exchange for a wooden passage permit at the city gate.

The more people the investigators questioned, the more their findings seemed separated from certainty by a sheet of thin paper. Lü An’s documents were false. The Shi family’s caravan had discrepancies in the number of travelers. Yao Chang’s household had hired a new groom named Lei Tong. Several Qiang officers transferred out of the Right Guard had still visited Yao’s home at the New Year. Those ties undoubtedly existed. Yet there was not one line in the case records proving that they amounted to rebellion.

Fu Hong laid the registers before Fu Jian. His father first asked what he had actually established. The crown prince described each finding. Fu Jian replied, “Lü An forged his leave documents: investigate him. Military supply permits have been falsified: investigate the permits. As for Yao Chang, do you have an order in his handwriting?”
“No.”
Fu Rong, who happened to be present, could not contain himself. “By the time we find one, I fear somebody will already have burned it for him.”
Fu Jian turned toward him. “Would you have me seal Yao’s residence tonight?”
“I would have Your Majesty change the locks on the palace gates first.”

Listening to the two men, Fu Hong suddenly remembered the drum signals issued incorrectly during the First Battalion’s inspection. He had believed then that finding the guilty drummer would settle everything. Only later had he discovered that the two signal flags had been too far apart for anyone to see clearly.

“Father,” he said, “let the Court of Justice investigate the caravans and forged credentials. From now on, let the two formations of the Right Guard alternate their duties, and let responsibility for verifying entry tokens at the gates be separated from the authority to issue orders from the armories. No regular guard unit should be allowed to enter the Court of Justice’s prison on the strength of a token from its own command. None of this requires us to declare General Yao guilty beforehand.”
Fu Jian watched him for a moment, then agreed. Fu Rong rested his hand against the edge of the table and, for once, did not press the matter further.

Several days later Lü An was detained. A Qiang merchant named Pu Sheng, who had escorted the leather shipments, was also brought to the Court of Justice prison. At first Pu Sheng repeated that he had only been trading horse hides to earn his living. But when the magistrates laid out the caravan wagon counts, the dates on which tenants had vanished from the estate, and several conflicting checkpoint certificates, he admitted carrying runaway tenants for the Shi family. He refused to say who had asked him to carry letters home.

On the fifth day of questioning, he mentioned Lei Tong. He claimed to have received from the groom at Yao’s residence a tiny folded paper for delivery to Beidi. The registrar had scarcely asked who was meant to receive it when Pu Sheng clutched his chest and began to struggle for breath. The questioning was suspended. The record stopped halfway down a page. That night the half-written sheet disappeared from the case file.

Fu Hong ordered Pu Sheng moved to a cell by himself, two guards replaced, and all sharp objects removed. He gave special instructions to inspect the credentials of anyone entering. Before dawn, something had gone wrong all the same.

Pu Sheng was found hanging from the low window bars. His sash was tight about his neck, his body on its knees, as though he had bowed his head against the wall in sleep. When the coroner removed the sash, he found several fresh fractures in the man’s fingers and dried black ink beneath his nails. Prisoners were supposed to have their sashes taken away on admission. Why had he still been wearing one after the transfer? One guard said he had been allowed it because he was cold; the other said he had never seen the strip of cloth. Their accounts contradicted each other.
“Who came here last night?” Fu Hong asked.

The guards said officers of the Right Guard had come looking for deserters, carrying Lü An’s token. Fu Hong immediately sent men to check Lü An in his other cell. He had not left it all night. Whether the paper was genuine, whether the token was a forgery, and whose hands had passed it on remained unknown.

The registrar was summoned to reconstruct the previous day’s testimony. Biting his lip, he recalled that Pu Sheng had spoken of a letter, and that the recipient’s name seemed to contain the character *Luo*. After that, the prisoner would say no more.
“Which Luo?” an officer of the Court of Justice demanded.
The registrar shook his head, tears falling onto his collar. “I did not hear clearly, my lord.”

Fu Hong looked at the blot of ink. Suddenly he was afraid that everyone would write the name he wished to see into the missing testimony. Many names contained the sound *Luo*, but there was only one Duke of Beihai. The dead man could no longer correct anyone.

“Find out every person who entered the prison last night, and every person who changed the locks,” he told the court officials. “Keep Pu Sheng’s body for another examination. Do not send someone to his death on the strength of one indistinct syllable.”

When the case file reached the palace, Fu Jian studied it for a long time. Several times Fu Rong seemed about to speak and restrained himself. At last the emperor ordered the Court of Justice to continue investigating and authorized the crown prince to draw up new procedures for rotating the palace guards. He did not sign an order to search Yao Chang’s house.
That same night, Yao Chang heard of Pu Sheng’s death in the stables.

Lei Tong was having a gray horse reshod. The household steward hurried in and knelt beside the wall, saying that the merchant was dead and his testimony had disappeared. “Who went there?” Yao Chang asked.
“We do not yet know.”
“I asked who sent them.”
The steward pressed his forehead to the ground. His voice trembled. “No message was sent from this house.”

Yao Chang watched the horse holding up its foreleg. The farrier hammered a fresh nail into the shoe; a few copper-colored sparks fell, and the animal shuddered in alarm. Lei Tong hurried to stroke its neck.
“Find out where the false token came from,” Yao Chang said. “And that half-page of testimony: who took it? When you learn, do not alarm anyone.”
“General, do you suspect someone was acting for us—”
“For whom?” Yao Chang asked softly.
The steward dared not finish.

The night wind came across the courtyard. One corner of the red wedding silk still hung beneath the eaves, its color darkened and fading. Lei Tong glanced at it without thinking, then bowed his head and held the horse steady. The young man knew only that the Lei and Yao families had become kin. He had yet to understand that a piece of paper he had carried was already connected to a man’s death in the prison of the Court of Justice.

Yao Chang let his right hand rest against the horse’s neck. He had always liked to employ such old followers: they remembered the favors he had done them and knew they had little place to turn in Chang’an. Now someone had killed to silence a witness without waiting for his word. If he could not find that hand, one day it might open a palace gate for him—or press a knife against his throat.

In the distance the third watch sounded from Weiyang Palace. Yao Chang told Lei Tong to lead the horse back to its stall, then went beneath the corridor, called for another lamp, and began asking about every person who had come and gone from his house, day by day.
